### Directions

![](media/diffuse/icecube-2013-zenith-dark.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 510px;" fig-alt="Redrawn IceCube 2013 zenith distribution after the starting-event selection, compared with atmospheric backgrounds and the fitted astrophysical component."}

Direction, energy and veto response constrain the background hypothesis together. · Redrawn from the vector artwork
:::

::::::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** In 2013 IceCube found more very energetic neutrinos than the atmosphere can make — the first cosmic neutrinos at TeV–PeV energies.

Results occupy 28–47 minutes. Allow about 90 seconds for The excess, using
Starting inside only if the veto needs another explanation. This is the original
2013 discovery sample, not a current spectrum measurement. The figure's orange
curve is its historical E^-2 astrophysical fit; the hatched band is the background
statistical and systematic uncertainty, and green and violet lines are atmospheric
neutrinos with benchmark charm and with the 90% CL charm limit. Deposited electromagnetic-equivalent
energy is the measured observable, not a universal parent-neutrino energy.

The 4.1-sigma result combines the 26 newly reported events with the earlier two
PeV events under the paper's benchmark atmospheric hypothesis. Prompt-charm
assumptions affect its significance. It is not obtained from a histogram excess
alone. The analysis uses charges, reconstructed energies and directions.
An entering-muon control sample constrains the residual muon background.
Atmospheric self-veto helps discriminate southern-sky neutrinos.

The selected population establishes an astrophysical component, without identifying
individual sources. Today's binned spectrum is shown after the GVD measurement.
Source: [IceCube (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.5238v2).
:::

**Say:** Baikal-GVD, in a completely different detector and medium, sees the same cosmic neutrino flux from below the horizon.

Allow about two minutes for Cascade energies and Spectrum. The growing detector
and season-dependent exposure enter the fit. This sample used clusters 1–12,
not the installed 2026 configuration. E_sh, hit multiplicity, zenith and quality
cuts select 18 cascades. The background estimate includes 1.9 atmospheric-neutrino
and 0.9 misreconstructed-muon events. The significance includes systematic effects.

The fit assumes equal flavour contributions and a single power law: gamma=2.64
(+0.09,-0.11), normalization 4.42 (+2.31,-1.29) times 1e-18 per flavour at
100 TeV, in GeV^-1 cm^-2 s^-1 sr^-1. The spectral figure redraws the 2025
publication comparison (digitized); its blue IceCube points were preliminary. The next slide
uses the finalized 2026 IceCube spectral-feature result. Parameter contours assume
a single power law and cover different analysis ranges. GVD's outer contour is
90%, while the IceCube outer contours are 95%; they are not identical intervals.

Source: [Baikal-GVD (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01893v2).
:::

### Glashow and flavour

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
![](media/diffuse/icecube-glashow-event-2021.jpg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 520px; --media-bg: #fff;" fig-alt="IceCube visualization of the December 2016 Glashow-resonance candidate: schematic of early muon light, the event view across the detector and photon arrival times at the two nearest sensors."}
:::
::: {.column width="41%"}
**Glashow resonance**

$$\bar\nu_e+e^-\to W^-\to\text{hadrons}$$

$$E_{\bar\nu}\simeq6.3\,\mathrm{PeV}$$

One shower, December 2016. Only antineutrinos can do this.

**Tau neutrinos**

Seven candidates: all three flavours arrive.

**Why it matters**

$pp$: $\ \bar\nu_e:\nu_e\approx1:1$

simple $p\gamma$: $\ \approx1:3.5$
:::
:::::

::: {.media-caption}
[IceCube, Nature 591, 220 (2021), Fig. 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15051) · [Tau neutrinos: IceCube, PRL 132, 151001 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02516)
:::

::::::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** The spectrum is not a straight line: it bends near 30 TeV, and at the top end nature even gives us a particle-physics resonance — one antineutrino hitting an electron at 6 PeV.

Spend about 90 seconds on Measured spectrum. The points are segmented flux fits
in true neutrino energy, assuming E^-2 within each band; they are not uncorrected
event counts. The BPL bands show 68% parameter uncertainties and sensitive ranges.
Arrow markers denote upper limits. All displayed source-averaged components and
normalizations are retained from the publication, without multiplying by three.

CF and MESE use complementary selections with different detector responses.
They are not two independent instruments; their significances must not be added.
BPL improves over SPL at 4.4 sigma for CF and 4.7 for MESE under the stated
likelihood test. A log parabola also improves the fit. A physical discontinuity
or a unique change of source population is not established. Point to the measured
shape before discussing possible target fields or the gamma-ray budget.

Glashow and flavour (optional, about one minute). The PEPE partially contained
sample covers May 2012–May 2017, 4.6 years of live time. The 8 December 2016
shower has visible energy 6.05±0.72 PeV, consistent with a hadronically decaying
6.3 PeV W⁻ after about 5% invisible energy. Early muon light at the nearest
sensors supports a hadronic W decay. An atmospheric-muon origin is rejected
a posteriori at more than 5 sigma. Against deep-inelastic CC/NC showers, the
visible-energy likelihood ratio gives p=0.01 (2.3 sigma, one-sided) under the
assumed astrophysical flux; 1.55 such events were expected. One event does not
measure the antineutrino fraction. The quoted 1:1 (pp) and 1:3.5 (simple
p-gamma, without multi-pion production) are the paper's anti-nu_e:nu_e ratios
at Earth. Strong magnetic fields can suppress anti-nu_e further.
Tau neutrinos: 9.7 years, convolutional-network selection, seven candidates
with an expected background of about 0.5 events. Absence of astrophysical tau
neutrinos is excluded at 5.1 sigma for the GlobalFit flux (5.2–5.5 for other
flux assumptions). The rate agrees with oscillation-averaged flavour mixing.

Sources: [IceCube (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22233v3);
[Glashow resonance, Nature 591, 220 (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03256-1),
[arXiv:2110.15051](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15051);
[tau neutrinos, PRL 132, 151001 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02516).
Figure credit: IceCube Collaboration (gallery adaptation of Nature Fig. 1).
:::

### Gamma rays

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="63%"}
![](media/galactic/galactic-gamma-diffuse.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 520px;" fig-alt="Redrawn published spectra of diffuse gamma rays from the Galactic plane between 10 TeV and 1 PeV: LHAASO-KM2A inner and outer Galaxy points from its tables, and Tibet AS-gamma points digitized from its Figure 4, shown as E to the 2.7 times the differential flux."}
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
**The same collisions**

$$\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma,\qquad \pi^\pm\to\nu\ \ldots$$

The Galactic plane glows in gamma rays up to $\sim1\,\mathrm{PeV}$.

**Tibet AS$\gamma$, 2021:** first diffuse gamma rays above $100\,\mathrm{TeV}$.

**LHAASO, 2023:** the spectrum from $10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ to $1\,\mathrm{PeV}$.
:::
:::::

::: {.media-caption}
Redrawn: [LHAASO, PRL 131, 151001 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05372v2), Tables S2–S3 · [Tibet AS$\gamma$, PRL 126, 141101 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05181v2), digitized from Fig. 4 · Different sky regions and source masks
:::

::::::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** Our own Galaxy shines in neutrinos. IceCube sees the glow of the plane, Baikal sees its highest-energy part, and gamma-ray telescopes see the same cosmic-ray collisions.

Spend about two minutes: IceCube, then Baikal-GVD, then Gamma rays. The
Animation tab is optional.

IceCube tab: Figure 1 of the 2023 Science paper, unchanged. Read the five rows
separately: optical, gamma rays, the pion-template neutrino prediction, the
expectation after detector effects, and observed pre-trial significance. The
bottom colour scale is significance, not intensity. The 4.5 sigma is the global
diffuse-template test including trials, not a pixel significance; individual
accelerators are not resolved. The cascade sample spans 500 GeV to multi-PeV.
ANTARES (Physics Letters B 841, 137951 (2023)): tracks and showers from the
region |l|<30°, |b|<2°, 1–100 TeV. The background-only hypothesis is disfavoured
at about 96% confidence: a hint, not a detection.

Baikal-GVD tab: cascades with reconstructed neutrino energy above 200 TeV,
spring 2018 to spring 2024 (about 26.8 one-cluster years). Simulations give
about 64% astrophysical purity. The model-independent test statistic is the
median absolute Galactic latitude, compared with skies whose right ascensions
are reshuffled. Observed 10.4° against 31.4° expected; p = 1.4e-2 (2.5 sigma),
with no trials. IceCube high-energy starting cascades above 200 TeV give
p = 8.7e-3 by the same method, public IceCube tracks (ICECAT, overlapping an
earlier compilation) p = 1.8e-3. All three combined: p = 3.4e-4 (3.6 sigma).
The rough flux estimate
above 200 TeV has large uncertainties but exceeds the standard cosmic-ray
templates used by IceCube. One of the eight cascades is the April 2021 event
near TXS 0506+056, shown later. The redrawn map uses Galactic coordinates,
those of the paper's Table 1; the paper's own map (Fig. 5) is equatorial and
also shows the IceCube events. The histogram recomputes the paper's Fig. 1 from
Table 1 (randomized right ascensions, declinations kept): p = 0.013, matching
the published 1.4e-2. Event coordinates are shown only graphically.

Animation tab. **Say:** This is how our Galaxy would glow in neutrinos seen from the Sun — and how Baikal checks it with its eight highest-energy cascades.
The sky map is a model Galaxy, not a measurement; the shuffling test uses the
published cascades, is recomputed and agrees with the paper.

Gamma rays tab: published points only, redrawn in the lecture style. LHAASO-KM2A
measures diffuse emission at 29.1 sigma (inner Galaxy) and 12.7 sigma (outer),
power-law index −2.99 in both, with the inner flux about three times the
prediction from locally measured cosmic rays and gas. Thick LHAASO bars are
statistical, thin bars include systematics. Regions: LHAASO inner 15°<l<125°,
outer 125°<l<235°; Tibet 25°<l<100° and 50°<l<200°; all |b|<5°. Tibet AS-gamma found 23 gamma-like
events above 398 TeV against 2.73 expected background (5.9 sigma), the highest
at 957 TeV, away from known sources: evidence for PeV cosmic rays spread through
the disk. Tibet bars are statistical. Source masks and regions differ, so the
two normalizations are not directly comparable. If the gamma rays come from pion
decays, a neutrino flux of similar size follows; the Baikal-GVD paper finds its
estimate closer to the Tibet-based expectation, possibly pointing to individual
PeVatrons, for example in Cygnus.

Sources: [IceCube, Science 380 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04427);
[ANTARES, PLB 841 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.11876);

[LHAASO, PRL 131 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05372v2);
[Tibet AS-gamma, PRL 126 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05181v2).
